text: Down in the basement the boiler knocked twice and went quiet, and the radiator in the front room answered with a long, thin hiss.
The wallpaper was a pattern of small brown baskets, faded almost to nothing in a square where the window let the streetlight in.
Four floors of cooking had soaked into the stairwell walls: onions, cabbage, and something fried in lard.
In the kitchen a tap dripped into a chipped enamel sink, one drop every few seconds, onto a rust mark the size of a thumbnail.
Four floors down, the avenue still carried the odd taxi, and its tires drummed on the cobbles in the stretch outside the building.
Behind the plaster the steam pipes ticked one by one as the steam went out of them, and below the window the street was still to the far corner.
Grey light came in off the air shaft and showed the cracks in the ceiling plaster, and somewhere toward the river a truck ground its gears.
The parlor ceiling kept its old plaster medallion, a ring of acanthus leaves with a brass chain dropping from the centre.
Tall windows faced the street, set in frames deep enough to sit in, their wood painted over more than once.
A marble mantel took up one wall, veined in grey, and the coal grate in it had long ago been bricked up and plastered.
Now and then the house made small sounds of its own: a joist easing over the hall, a pipe knocking behind the wainscot.
Across the street the stoops ran down the block in an even line, each with its iron railing, under streetlamps spaced every few houses.
Every radiator in the house had gone silent, and through the ceiling came the faint tick of a clock on the floor above.
Pale light found the stained glass over the front door and put a smear of red and amber down the length of the hall.
The drugstore's smells came up through the floorboards: vanilla and cherry syrup, and under them something sharper, camphor or carbolic.
Bare pine stairs climbed from the street, worn pale down the middle, with a rubber tread tacked to every third one.
Out the back window a fire escape zigzagged down the rear wall into a yard with a clothes pole and a single ailanthus tree.
Its ceiling was pressed tin, painted cream, with one corner gone brown with rust where a vent pipe ran up through to the roof.
Down below, the drugstore's sign threw a green glow on the pavement, and its hum came faintly up through the floor.
Somewhere in the drugstore a refrigerator motor cut in, ran for a minute, and cut out again, the only thing in the building making a sound.
First light showed in the front window, and at the corner a delivery truck let its tailgate fall with a bang that carried up three flights.
The hall carpet ran the length of the floor, red gone brown, patterned with a vine that repeated every few yards.
An elevator shaft ran up beside the room, and its cables hummed faintly in the wall even while the car sat idle somewhere below.
A transom over the door let in a thin bar of light from the hall, and a steam pipe rose straight through the corner to the floor above.
Hotel wallpaper, the same on every floor, cream with a gold stripe, had lifted at the seams where the radiator dried it out.
Out the window, the hotel's sign lit the fire escape red, and the street below still had a taxi or two nosing along it.
The steam had been turned down, and the radiator ticked as it cooled, a dry sound in the plaster behind it.
Across the airshaft the next roof went from black to grey, and pigeons started moving along its ledge in short hops.
The back house was older than the building in front of it, with walls a foot thick and low ceilings of rough plank.
From its window the only view was the rear of the front house, four stories of brick and a ladder of fire escapes.
Outside in the little yard stood a pump with an iron handle painted green, left from the days before the city ran water back here.
Its floors sloped toward the lane, and the boards were so old they had worn into ridges around every knot.
Over the roofs of the front house, the avenue's signs made a dull band of light along the top of the wall.
Water ran somewhere in the old pipes under the yard, a slow gurgle, and after it there was no sound back here at all.
Daylight reached the yard late, coming down past the front house, and a sparrow set up a racket on the pump handle.
Water tanks stood on iron legs at either end of the roof, their wooden staves banded with hoops of rusted steel.
Underfoot the tar was patched in a dozen places, and a low brick parapet ran round the edge, knee high and crumbling at the corners.
A pigeon coop of lath and chicken wire sat against the chimney stack, and the birds inside shifted and muttered on their perches.
Chimney pots stood up in rows across the neighbouring roofs, and between them clotheslines ran from pole to pole.
Below the parapet the avenue signs threw red and white up the fronts of the buildings, and the traffic noise came up thin and far off.
From up here the whole block lay dark below the parapet, and the only sound was one of the tanks dripping into its pan.
Over the river the sky had gone pale, and the water tanks stood out black against it while pigeons circled off the coop.
The delicatessen's back step gave onto the alley, and the air behind it smelled of brine, smoked fish, and sour pickles.
Ash cans lined one wall, dented tin with the lids chained on, and a rat went along the gutter between them.
Fire escapes climbed both walls, and their iron landings threw ladder shadows down across the brick paving.
By the delicatessen's step stood crates of pickle jars, and a grease barrel beside them had its lid wired down.
At the mouth of the alley the street was still bright, and a taxi went by across the gap without slowing.
A cat sat on the lid of an ash can and watched the alley, and high on one of the fire escapes a radio played low behind a window.
Morning came down between the walls grey and slow, and out front a truck backed up to the delicatessen with its motor grumbling.
The tailor's pressing had left its smell in the stair: hot wool, scorched cotton, and steam.
A panel of frosted glass was set in the office door, and the radiator under the window was painted silver and knocked when the steam came up.
A calendar from a coal merchant hung by the window, and below it the plaster had cracked in a long line down to the baseboard.
Outside, the tailor's sign hung from its iron bracket over the pavement, a pair of shears painted gold on a black board.
Across the street a shop sign buzzed and flickered, and its light came through the window in a blue stripe across the floorboards.
With the radiator finished knocking, the only sound in the building was a faucet dripping into a sink in the washroom down the hall.
Dawn came grey through the frosted glass, and down in the street a truck rattled over the cobbles toward the market.
The shed smelled of tar and hemp and river water, and under the corrugated roof the rafters were white with gull droppings.
Coils of heavy hawser lay along the stringpiece, and iron bollards stood at intervals, worn bright where the lines had run.
Under the planks the river slapped at the pilings, and the whole pier gave a slow creak whenever the tide pulled against it.
Crates were stacked to the rafters along the back, stencilled with the names of foreign ports, and a cargo hook hung from its chain overhead.
A tug's lamp slid slowly downstream past the end of the pier, and its wash came in against the pilings a minute later.
The tide had turned, and the river sucked and slapped under the stringpiece, loud beneath the shed roof with no other sound to cover it.
Under the edge of the shed roof the water had gone pale, and gulls had started walking the stringpiece.
Clotheslines crossed the yard in rows from pole to pole, hung with wooden clothespins gone grey with age.
The ground was packed dirt with a drain in the middle, and a smell of lye soap and starch came through the laundry’s back wall.
A boiler vent stuck out of the laundry wall at head height, streaked white with scale, and the brick around it was stained dark.
Wooden washtubs leaned against the fence, their staves bleached almost white, beside an iron wringer with a crank handle.
Behind the laundry wall the boiler still ticked, and the vent gave off a last faint smell of soap into the yard.
Under the lines the yard was dark to the fence, and nothing made a sound but the drain in the middle, gurgling now and then.
As the sky over the fence went pale, the laundry's boiler fire started up inside with a roar that shook the vent pipe.
Bare boards made the stairs up, with a banister loose in its posts, and the landing smelled of kerosene and floor soap.
Every door on the third-floor landing had a number painted on it and nothing else, and the paint was chipped to the wood.
Its one window looked onto the backs of the tenements behind, row on row of fire escapes hung with bedding and washlines.
A gas ring and a small sink shared one wall, and the gas pipe ran up the plaster in plain sight, painted over the same tan as the wall.
Across the air shaft a radio played dance music low behind a drawn shade, a band going round and round the same tune.
A pipe in the wall knocked now and then, and otherwise the third floor had gone silent all the way down to the street door.
Early grey came through the window over the rear tenements, and the pigeons on the fire escape opposite were out on the rail.
Marble ran underfoot in black and white squares, and a bank of brass mailboxes along one wall had been polished until the numbers wore faint.
A tall mirror in a gilt frame hung opposite the entrance, and a rubber mat inside the doors had a single initial worked into it.
The elevator gate was brass latticework, and above it a half-moon dial with an arrow showed which floor the car was on.
Floor wax and brass polish were what the vestibule smelled of, and a radiator behind a grille of pierced brass hissed under the mirror.
Through the glass of the street doors the avenue's signs showed red and white, and the marble squares took a faint wash of their colour.
An elevator motor high up the shaft hummed for a moment and stopped, and the vestibule's radiator had cooled to an occasional tick.
Grey daylight came through the street doors and lay across the marble, and the mailboxes lost their shine in it.
The room looked onto an air shaft, and across it, close enough to touch with a broom handle, stood another building's windowless brick.
A card of house rules was tacked to the back of the door, lettered by hand, with the price of a bath and the hours of the kitchen.
New wallpaper had been hung over old, and at the seams the older pattern showed through, small roses under large ferns.
A brown water stain spread across one corner of the ceiling, under a bathroom on the floor above.
Down the hall a toilet tank hissed without ever quite shutting off, and a radiator somewhere in the house knocked twice.
Out on the landing the stair creaked once as the old wood settled, and after that there was only the tick of the radiator cooling.
Grey came down the air shaft, just enough to show the roses in the wallpaper, and from the kitchen below rose the smell of coffee.
A brass rail ran along the foot of the bar at ankle height, and the floor under it was scattered with sawdust.
Behind the bar the mirror had gone cloudy at the edges, and the tap handles stood in a row in front of it, black and white porcelain.
Over the lunch counter hung a framed picture of a racehorse, and beside it a jar of pickled eggs sat on the wood.
Beer, sawdust, and the onions on the lunch counter were what the place smelled of, and a beer sign in the window buzzed in red script.
A taxi's horn sounded twice in the street, and under the bar the beer coils gurgled as the lines settled.
The clock over the door ticked against a tap dripping into the trough under the bar, and neither sound hurried.
Daylight came in past the painted lettering on the front window, and it made the tile floor look older than it had under the bulbs.
The ceiling was low and crossed with the hat shop's pipes, and a string of coloured bulbs ran along the bar beneath them.
Brick walls had been whitewashed once and gone yellow, and the air carried coal smoke from the furnace room next door.
A slot was cut in the door at eye height, with an iron cover on a slide, and the stair down to it was six steps of worn stone.
Behind the bar, clean glasses stood in rows under a mirror whose silvering had gone, spotted black in the corners.
The coloured bulbs over the bar gave the room a red and green cast, and a furnace behind the wall thumped every so often.
A drain in the wall gurgled and went quiet, and overhead the hat shop's floor gave a single long creak as the building settled.
No daylight got down this far, but the smell of the bakery two doors along came in through the vent, sweet and yeasty.
Red carpet ran from the revolving door to the elevators, worn to the backing down the middle, held at the steps by brass rods.
Pigeonholes filled the wall behind the desk, one for every room, with a small brass number under each.
Marble columns held up a ceiling of gilded plaster, and years of cigar smoke had darkened the rosettes nearest the lamps.
A cigar counter stood by the elevators under a glass top, and the lobby smelled of floor polish and the steam from the radiators.
Behind a leather settee a radiator hissed, and through the front windows the avenue's signs threw red and gold across the carpet.
Over the desk the lobby clock ticked, loud against all that marble, and somewhere under the floor a boiler gave a long, low groan.
Dawn made the gilt on the ceiling look cheap as it came through the tall front windows, and a truck pulled in at the curb outside.
The stand was a wooden box with a corrugated tin roof and a wire strung across its front, with magazines clipped along it under a single bulb.
Chewing gum and cigars sat in a glass case under the counter, and along the side hung racks of detective magazines and movie monthlies.
Behind the stand rose a lamppost at the curb, and a fire hydrant stood beside it, painted red and chipped down to the iron.
A subway grating ran along the curb beside the stand, and warm air came up through it with a smell of iron and grease.
Above the crossing the traffic signal clicked from green to red, and the stand's bulb hummed on its wire over the magazine covers.
The traffic light on the corner went on changing, red to green and back, and its click was the loudest sound at the crossing.
Up the avenue the light went pale block by block, and a street-cleaning truck went by along the gutter, its brushes turning, spraying water at the curb.
A wall of little glass doors filled one side of the room, each with a slot and a knob, and behind them sat pie and sandwiches on white plates.
Coffee came from brass spouts shaped into dolphins' heads, and the whole room smelled of it, with baked beans underneath.
Marble topped the tables, the floor was small white hexagonal tile, and every surface in the place had been rubbed to a shine.
Chrome and glass ran everywhere, and behind the wall of compartments the steam tables gave off a smell of creamed spinach.
Under the ceiling lights the chrome of the coffee urns shone, and the steam tables behind the wall hissed now and then.
A refrigerator motor ran somewhere behind the wall of little doors, a steady drone under the ticking of a clock over the entrance.
Grey from the street mixed with the white of the ceiling lights, and the coffee smell had turned fresh.
The lobby carpet was a pattern of red and gold scrolls, and gilt plaster cherubs looked down from the corners of the ceiling.
Frames along the lobby walls held posters for coming attractions, painted faces two feet high over lettering in red and yellow.
Stale cigarette smoke hung in the auditorium, and the heavy velvet curtain over the screen had faded along its folds.
Red exit signs glowed at the ends of the aisles, and the seats ran down toward the stage in long curved rows of worn plush.
Up in the projection booth a fan turned in the wall, and the smell of warm film and hot carbon came down the booth stair.
Plaster and gilt ticked and creaked as the big auditorium lost its warmth, and each small sound carried up to the balcony rail.
A line of grey showed around the edges of the lobby doors, and a truck stopped under the marquee outside and idled.
A mirror ball hung from the middle of the ceiling, and the maple floor under it had been waxed to a hard shine.
At the far end stood the bandstand, with music stands in rows, their fronts painted with a lyre in gold.
Crepe streamers hung from the balcony rail, and the rail itself had been painted gold, peeling now at the posts.
Floor wax, talcum, and stale perfume filled the hall, and the ceiling was painted dark blue with gold stars.
A radiator hissed under the bandstand, and in the mirror ball's little squares the room showed a hundred times over.
Now and then the big floor gave a creak as the boards settled, and the tall windows along one side showed only the room's own reflection.
Early light came in the tall windows and fell across the dance floor, showing every scuff in the wax.
The soda fountain ran along one side, marble counter and nickel taps, and the air smelled of chocolate syrup and orange phosphate.
Show cards were propped along the mirror behind the fountain, lettered by hand in red and blue: sodas, malteds, egg creams.
In the window, two tall glass globes of coloured water, one red and one green, stood on pedestals over a display of toothbrushes and talcum tins.
A weighing scale stood by the door with a round mirror in its front, and the floor was small black and white tiles, worn grey by the fountain stools.
A ceiling fan hung still over the fountain, and the drink cooler behind the counter shuddered each time its motor cut in.
Behind the prescription counter a small radio played dance music very low, and the syrup pumps at the fountain gave off their sweet smell.
Past the coloured globes in the window the first light came in faint, and it threw a little red and green across the tiles.
A line was painted along the curb for the cabs, and the paint had worn through to concrete where the front wheels always stopped.
Above the stand the theatre's marquee ran out over the pavement, its underside studded with rows of bulbs.
Exhaust and hot radiators were what the curb smelled of, and the cabs sat nose to tail with their roof lights showing.
Brass stanchions stood along the pavement for the theatre's lines, and a signpost at the front of the stand read CABS in white lettering.
The first cab in line had its motor idling, and its meter flag stood up, white, in the light from the marquee.
Along the stand the parked motors had gone quiet one by one, and the gutter carried the smell of gasoline down to the corner drain.
Grey daylight crept up the street under the marquee, and a produce truck went past the stand heading for the markets.
Each tread was worn into a shallow dip at the middle, and the banister had been rubbed down to bare wood along its whole length.
Every landing had its own smell: garlic on the second, boiled cabbage on the third, and on the fourth, kerosene.
Brown paint covered the walls to shoulder height and green above, and the green had flaked away in patches the size of a hand.
At the top a skylight of wired glass capped the stairwell, and from the bottom the stairs could be seen winding all the way up to it.
Behind one door on the second landing a radio played a dance band, and a bare bulb on the landing above buzzed on its wire.
Water pipes along the stairwell wall knocked as something drained through them from the top floor, and then the stairs went silent.
Through the skylight came the first grey, and it showed the dip in every tread, one after another, all the way to the bottom.
Green-shaded lamps hung low over the tables, and under them the cloth was a hard, even green, marked with chalk dust at the corners.
Cue racks lined the walls, and strings of scoring beads hung on wires overhead, stretched across the room from wall to wall.
The pool hall smelled of talcum, cigar smoke, and the linseed oil used on the cues.
A slate by the counter carried a chalked list of the house rules, and a brass spittoon stood beside every other table.
The pressed tin overhead had gone brown with smoke, and an exhaust fan high in the rear wall turned slowly, pulling the haze toward it.
Below street level no sound came in from outside, and the only noise was a pipe dripping into a bucket behind the counter.
Pale light reached the half-windows high in the front wall, at pavement level, and showed the smoke still hanging over the tables.
Clocks covered one wall of the back room, a dozen or more, each ticking at its own pace and none of them agreeing.
Musical instruments hung from hooks in the ceiling: a trumpet, two banjos, a saxophone gone green at the joints.
Mothballs, brass polish, and machine oil were what the back room smelled of, from the sewing machines stacked against the far wall.
Shelves ran floor to ceiling, packed with radios and cameras, and a stuffed owl under a glass dome sat on the top one.
One of the radios on the shelves played dance music low, and its dial glowed amber among the dark faces of the others.
A tailor's dummy stood in the corner in a half-finished jacket, and the refrigerator in the shop next door hummed through the wall.
A barred window high in the back wall let in a square of grey, and it fell across the shelves, catching the brass of a tuba.
The room smelled of peanut oil, soy, and ginger, and under it came the starch and steam of the laundry below.
Red and gold lettering ran across the front windows, and lanterns of red silk hung from the ceiling on thin chains.
A calendar from a grocer hung by the kitchen door with a tiger on it, and under it a fish tank bubbled in the corner.
Oilcloth covered the tables, white with a red border, and a kitchen fan in the back wall turned with a steady rattle.
Behind the swinging door the kitchen range still roared, and the smell of frying onions came through with every turn of the fan.
Down through the floor came the tick of the laundry's pipes cooling, and in the corner the fish tank's pump hummed on and on.
Through the red lettering on the windows the sky showed grey, and steam began to rise again through the floorboards from the laundry's first wash.
A horsehair sofa stood against the wall under a framed sampler, and lace covers were pinned over its arms and back.
The parlour smelled of furniture polish and of the cabbage boiled earlier at the back of the house.
A glass dome of wax fruit sat on the mantelpiece beside a black marble clock with gilt columns.
Its ceiling fixture had been gas once and was wired for electric light now, and the old pipe still stood out from the plaster, painted over.
A radiator under the bay window hissed and knocked, and through the lace curtains the streetlamp outside made a pattern on the carpet.
Under the wallpaper the old lath and plaster ticked and shifted, and out in the hall the brass rods of the stair runner caught the streetlamp.
The lace at the bay window went grey with the first light, and down the hall the smell of coffee and frying bacon began to come from the kitchen.
Three chairs of white porcelain and red leather faced a long mirror, and the mirror on the back wall gave them back again, row on row.
Bay rum and talcum were the shop's smells, with a sharp note of witch hazel from the counter.
A tall jar of blue disinfectant held a stand of combs, and beside it sat a nickel towel steamer with a hinged lid.
In the window the striped pole turned slowly in its glass case, and its motor gave a faint whine through the wall.
The streetlamp outside laid the shop's window lettering backward across the linoleum, and a radiator under the window ticked as the steam came up.
A tap at the shampoo basin dripped into the porcelain, slow and even, and the mirrors held the dark of the street outside.
Grey came in over the lettering on the window and found the chrome of the chairs, and a delivery van stopped at the curb with its motor running.
Oil stains covered the concrete floor in overlapping rings, and the air was thick with gasoline, rubber, and exhaust.
A grease pit ran down the middle of the bay, lined with brick and black with old oil, with a work lamp hanging over it on a hook.
A red gas pump stood by the entrance with a glass globe on top, and an air hose hung in loops on a peg beside it.
Tires hung on pegs along the back wall, and the ramp to the upper level curved up past a painted sign that said SLOW.
An engine somewhere along the row ticked as it cooled, and the compressor in the corner cut in with a thump and a long hiss.
Long rows of hoods and fenders shone faintly under the hanging bulbs, and the compressor held its pressure without a sound.
Daylight showed in a strip above the big rolling door, and a truck downshifted outside with a clash of gears.
The platform was planks laid across iron girders, with gaps between them wide enough to see the street two stories down.
Iron columns, riveted at every joint, held up a wooden canopy over the platform, and the green paint on them had flaked to rust.
A gum machine with a little mirror on its front was bolted to a column, and an enamel station sign hung above it.
From the platform the view ran straight into second-floor windows across the street, a row of shades and curtains a few yards off.
Turnstiles of brass and wood stood in a row by the change booth, and a bulb in a wire cage hung over them, buzzing.
The rails ran off in both directions, silver under the signal lamps, and the iron under the platform gave a small tick now and then.
Pale sky showed between the canopy and the rooftops, and below, a truck rolled along between the columns, loud in all that iron.
The benches were green slats on iron legs cast into lion's paws, and the arms had lost their paint to grey wood.
Plane trees stood behind the benches, their bark peeling in patches of grey and cream, and the gravel path in front was mixed with cinders.
A drinking fountain of green bronze stood at the end of the row, and the basin under its spout was stained with verdigris.
Iron hoops edged the grass along the path, knee high, and pigeons worked the gravel between the benches for crumbs.
The nearest lamp stood on an iron post past the last bench, and beyond its circle the paths went off dark between the trees.
A granite monument stood in the middle of the square on a stepped base, and from the benches only its outline showed against the lamps beyond.
Between the plane trees the light turned pale, and sparrows started up in the branches over the benches, loud in the square.
The landing was a wooden ramp sloping down to the water between two rows of pilings, black with tar and scraped pale by the ferries’ hulls.
Heavy chains ran from the hinged ramp up to counterweights in iron towers on either side, and they creaked whenever the river lifted the float.
Tar, coal smoke, and brackish water were the smells down here, and the river sucked at the pilings under the ramp.
At the head of the slip stood the ferry house, a wooden building with a clock in its gable and benches behind its windows.
Across the river the far shore showed as a line of lights along the water, broken wherever the piers ran out.
The float bumped against the pilings with a slow, heavy knock, over and over, and the river ran past the slip black and quick.
Pale light spread over the water from the east, and gulls sat along the tops of the pilings facing into it.
The kiosk was iron and glass, with a peaked roof of cast iron and a stair going down under it into a tiled passage.
Warm air came up the stair from below, smelling of iron dust, grease, and the creosote on the ties.
White tile lined the stairwell walls below street level, with a border of blue and a mosaic plaque at the landing.
Brass handrails ran down both sides of the stair, and an enamel sign at the top said SUBWAY in white on dark green.
Two iron lamp posts flanked the kiosk, each with a round glass globe, and their light went a few steps down the stair and stopped.
Down the stair the tiled passage ran off under bare bulbs, and the only sound coming up from it was a drip somewhere out of sight.
Grey light lay on the glass panels of the kiosk, and across the intersection a bakery van was making its first stop.
Votive candles burned in rows of red glass cups on an iron stand, and the air was heavy with wax and old incense.
A plaster saint stood in a niche over the small altar, painted in blue and gold, one hand raised.
A kneeling rail of dark oak ran across the front, its cushion worn through in two places to the horsehair underneath.
A marble font for holy water stood by the door, and the walls above the wainscot were painted a pale blue with gilt borders.
The candle flames in their red cups stood straight and still, and the stand under them was crusted with years of dripped wax.
A candle guttered in its cup and went out with a small hiss, and the smell of hot wax rose off the stand.
The stained glass window began to show its colours, and it put blue and red on the stone floor in front of the altar rail.
The hall smelled of bread from the bakery below, and the floorboards were warm from the ovens.
A framed charter hung behind the lectern, and beside it a painted banner of the local, gold fringe on red silk, with two clasped hands.
One long room made up the hall, with a low stage at the far end, a flag in a stand, and a coffee urn on a trestle table.
Tall windows along the street side had their lower panes painted over, and the upper panes showed the tops of the buildings opposite.
By the stage a radiator hissed, and the smell of the bakery's last batch still hung under the high plaster ceiling.
Down below, the bakery's mixing machine started with a grind and a thump, and the floor of the hall shook faintly under it.
Light came in pale over the painted-out lower panes, and the smell of fresh bread came up through the boards thick and warm.
